claim: Failure to pay the tax reported due on a CT-1040 by the due date draws a one-time penalty of 10% of the amount due and unpaid. It is not monthly and has no further cap. DRS's page says the same: 'The penalty for late payment or underpayment of income or use tax is 10% of the tax due.' If an extension to file was granted, the penalty is avoided by paying at least 90% by the original due date and the balance by the extended date.
sourceDate: Conn. Gen. Stat. 12-735(a), General Statutes revised to Jan 1 2025 (2026 Supplement note); DRS page https://portal.ct.gov/drs/individuals/resident-income-tax/tax-information read 2026-10-10 (covers tax year 2025)
establishes: CT late-payment penalty = one-time 10% of unpaid tax
uncertainty: high confidence: the statute text and the DRS page agree
designImplication: Model CT as a single 10% hit at the due date, not a penalty that grows each month. Interest supplies the time cost.

claim: CT has no separate monthly late-filing penalty for a return that shows tax due. The 10% penalty under 12-735(a) covers late payment and late filing. If DRS has to file a return for a non-filer (after 3 months), the penalty is 10% of the tax or $50, whichever is greater. A taxpayer cannot be charged under both 12-735(a) and (b) for the same period. If no tax is due, DRS 'may impose a $50 penalty' for a late return.
value: 10% or $50 minimum (DRS-prepared return); $50 if no tax due
sourceDate: Conn. Gen. Stat. 12-735(b); DRS Tax Information page read 2026-10-10
establishes: Late filing and late payment do not stack in CT: there is one 10% penalty, with a $50 floor only on a DRS-prepared return
uncertainty: high confidence: statute text quoted directly
designImplication: For CT, filing late but paying in full costs nothing beyond the possible $50. Filing on time without paying costs the same 10% as filing late without paying.

claim: Unpaid CT income tax bears interest at 1% per month or fraction of a month (12% a year) from the due date until paid. The rate is fixed by statute and is not adjusted each quarter. It is simple interest on the tax: a 1994/95 amendment limited interest to the tax 'rather than on tax and penalty'. Interest cannot be waived. Any part of a month counts as a full month.
sourceDate: Conn. Gen. Stat. 12-735(a)-(b) and history note (May Sp. Sess. P.A. 94-4); DRS Tax Information page read 2026-10-10
establishes: CT interest = 1%/month, simple, on tax only, not on penalty, not compounded
uncertainty: high confidence on the rate. Medium confidence on 'no interest on penalty': it comes from the statute's history note and from the wording 'such amount' (the tax). DRS publishes no explicit statement
designImplication: CT interest is the steepest of the three (12%/yr) but grows linearly. Round any partial month up to a whole month.

claim: DRS Installment Agreement for individuals has these conditions: the account is not in collection status with DRS or a collection agency; it is not under warrant, bankruptcy or criminal investigation; all tax returns are filed; current liabilities are $50,000 or less; and the term does not exceed 12 months. A DRS myconneCT tutorial says a plan runs for at least 2 and at most 12 months. An older search snippet of the same DRS page said $10,000; the live page read on 2026-10-10 says $50,000.
sourceDate: DRS 'Other Helpful Information' page read 2026-10-10 (page carries tax-year-2025 content; no revision date shown)
establishes: CT plan: up to $50,000, at most 12 months, all returns filed, and not already in collections or under warrant
uncertainty: medium-high confidence: primary source, but no revision date, and an indexed copy showed $10,000. The 2-month minimum comes from a DRS tutorial PDF found by search and was not re-read
designImplication: CT is the strictest plan: 12 months at most, and an account already under warrant cannot get one online. A player must ask early, before the warrant.

claim: Individuals apply online in myconneCT (Summary tab, then 'Request Payment Plan'). Anyone who fails the eligibility tests must phone a Revenue Agent at 860-297-4936. A separate hardship route exists: Form CT-1127 asks for a 6-month extension of time to pay. It must be filed by the original due date. Penalty is waived if the tax is paid by the end of the extension, but interest still runs from the original due date.
value: myconneCT online; CT-1127 for 6-month hardship extension
sourceDate: DRS pages read 2026-10-10; CT-1127 rule from DRS search snippet (portal.ct.gov Tax Information)
establishes: How to apply. CT-1127 is a separate penalty-free deferral with a 6-month cap
uncertainty: high confidence on the online route. Medium confidence on the CT-1127 details, which came from a DRS search snippet and were not re-read in full
designImplication: CT gives two levers: an extension asked for before the due date (no penalty, interest only) and a short plan after the bill arrives.

Interest keeps accruing by statute, because 12-735 runs interest 'until the date of payment'.
sourceDate: searched 2026-10-10

claim: DRS: 'Even if you have an established payment plan with the Department ... any refund due you from the IRS and or State of Connecticut will be applied to your bill and it is not considered your monthly installment.' The Federal Offset page adds that DRS will keep pursuing federal offset while a payment plan is current, as long as any balance is unpaid.
sourceDate: DRS pages read 2026-10-10
establishes: A CT plan does not protect refunds. Both federal and state refunds are taken, and monthly payments are still due
uncertainty: high confidence: explicit DRS text
designImplication: Offset a CT plan balance with both refunds, and do not let an offset count as that month's installment.

topic: state refund offset (other years / other debts)
claim: The Commissioner 'may credit an overpayment of income tax ... against any liability in respect of any tax imposed by this state' (12-739). Under 12-39g, any amount the state owes a taxpayer (other than state-employee wages) is reduced by taxes unpaid more than 30 days past due and not under appeal. Under 12-742, refunds are also withheld for debts to other state agencies.
sourceDate: Conn. Gen. Stat. 12-739, 12-742 (chap. 229) and 12-39g (chap. 202), revised to Jan 1 2025
establishes: A CT refund from one year pays a CT balance from another
uncertainty: high confidence: statute text
designImplication: Apply next year's CT refund automatically to an open CT balance.

claim: CT takes part in the Treasury Offset Program for past-due, legally enforceable CT income tax. DRS sends a Notice of Intent to Offset by certified mail. The taxpayer has 60 days to pay in full (including ongoing interest) or request a review. After that, DRS refers the debt and the federal refund is offset. DRS charges no fee for the offset. It takes at least 4 weeks for the payment to post, and offsets can recur in later years.
sourceDate: DRS Federal Offset Program page read 2026-10-10 (no revision date shown)
establishes: CT debts are offset against federal refunds after a 60-day certified notice, with no fee
uncertainty: high confidence: primary DRS page
designImplication: A CT balance left unresolved 60 days after the notice eats the next federal refund.

claim: If tax is unpaid 30 days after its due date, DRS may issue a tax warrant for distraint on real or personal property, which has the force of a court execution (12-35(a)(3)). A warrant on intangibles (bank accounts, wages, receivables) needs written notice of intent at least 30 days before it is issued. It may order the third party to keep delivering amounts for 180 days or until paid. Serving officers' fees are twice the statutory fees ($5 minimum) and are paid first from what is collected. Tax, penalty and interest are a lien on CT real estate from the last day of the taxable year (12-734). Collection is barred 10 years after the return is filed or the assessment is final, unless a lien is recorded or an agreement exists.
sourceDate: Conn. Gen. Stat. 12-35, 12-734, revised to Jan 1 2025
establishes: CT enforcement: warrant possible at day 30 or later; bank or wage seizure needs a 30-day notice of intent first; 180-day continuing levy
uncertainty: high confidence on the statutory floors. Not found: the names and timing of DRS billing notices before the notice of intent, and how long DRS actually waits in practice
designImplication: Earliest CT levy is about day 60 (30 days past due, then 30-day notice). Actual timing is probably longer, but the statute sets the floor.

claim: By statute, and 'notwithstanding any instructions by the payor', a partial payment goes first to penalties (unless a penalty waiver was requested and approved), then for periods ending on or after Dec 31 2019 to interest, and then to tax.
sourceDate: Conn. Gen. Stat. 12-39h, revised to Jan 1 2025
establishes: CT applies payments penalty, then interest, then tax
uncertainty: high confidence: statute text
designImplication: Because interest runs on tax only, CT's order means partial payments leave the interest-bearing principal in place longest. A player paying in pieces cuts interest last.

claim: 5% of the tax due for each month or part of a month the return is late, up to 25%. If the return is more than 60 days late, the minimum penalty is the lesser of $100 or 100% of the tax due.
sourceDate: DTF page updated 2025-10-23; NY Tax Law 685(a)(1) (nysenate.gov, read 2026-10-10)
establishes: NY late-filing penalty
uncertainty: high confidence: DTF page and statute agree
designImplication: NY late filing costs 5% a month and reaches the 25% cap in the fifth month.

claim: 0.5% of the unpaid amount for each month or part of a month it is not paid, up to 25%.
sourceDate: DTF page updated 2025-10-23; NY Tax Law 685(a)(2)
establishes: NY late-payment penalty: monthly, 25% cap (reached at 50 months)
uncertainty: high confidence
designImplication: Accrue NY late payment monthly on the remaining unpaid balance, so paying down the balance lowers each later month's charge.

claim: Both can apply, but for any month in which both apply, the late-filing addition is reduced by the late-payment addition (Tax Law 685(a)(3)). The reduction cannot take the late-filing penalty below the over-60-days minimum. In effect, a month with both costs 5%, not 5.5%.
value: late-filing reduced by late-payment for overlapping months
sourceDate: NY Tax Law 685(a)(3), nysenate.gov read 2026-10-10
establishes: NY penalties do not fully stack, which mirrors the IRS rule
uncertainty: high confidence: statute, though read through a summarizing fetch rather than a raw copy
designImplication: Combined NY penalty in an overlapping month is 5%; after the 25% filing cap, only the 0.5% payment penalty keeps running.

claim: Personal income tax late payment or underpayment interest for 10/1/2026 to 12/31/2026 is 9.5% a year, compounded daily. Refunds earn 6%. The rate is reset each quarter.
sourceDate: DTF release dated 2026-08-20 for Q4 2026
establishes: NY Q4 2026 underpayment rate 9.5%, daily compounding
uncertainty: high confidence: primary DTF page
designImplication: NY interest is lower per year than CT's but compounds daily. Use 9.5% for late 2026 and expect a quarterly reset.

claim: The statutory underpayment rate is the federal short-term rate plus 5.5 points, with a floor of 7.5% a year, compounded daily (Tax Law 697(j)). Interest is charged on a penalty or addition to tax only if it is not paid within 21 calendar days after notice and demand (10 business days if $100,000 or more) (Tax Law 684(g)).
sourceDate: NY Tax Law 684(g), 697(j), nysenate.gov read 2026-10-10
establishes: NY interest on penalties starts only after 21 days unpaid past notice and demand
uncertainty: high confidence on the rule. Medium confidence on the exact wording, which came through a summarizing fetch
designImplication: Paying a NY bill within 21 days of the notice keeps the penalties interest-free. That gives a real reward for prompt payment.

claim: Through Online Services, an individual can request an IPA for a balance of $20,000 or less, with 36 or fewer monthly payments. Larger balances or longer terms must be requested by phone (518-457-5434). The department may require Form DTF-5, Statement of Financial Condition. Conditions of an IPA: file all returns and pay all future taxes on time. No maximum term for phone IPAs is published.
sourceDate: DTF IPA page updated 2025-07-25; IPA info page updated 2025-12-11; Publication 131 (7/25)
establishes: NY: $20,000 / 36 months online; more by phone with financial disclosure
uncertainty: high confidence on the online limits. The cap for phone IPAs was not found
designImplication: A NY plan is self-serve below $20k and 36 months. Above that, model a slower negotiated path that needs a financial statement.

topic: IPA fee, approval, default, refunds, new balances
claim: No setup fee is published, and DTF says it charges no late fees on missed IPA payments. Penalty and interest keep accruing on the unpaid balance for the life of the IPA. A missed payment is a default only if it is not made up by the next due date along with that month's regular payment. DTF gives at least 30 days' written notice before terminating or modifying, except when collection is in jeopardy. After termination it may file a warrant, garnish wages or levy. New bills 'do not automatically roll into your existing IPA': they must be paid separately or a new combined IPA requested. State and federal refunds may be offset during the IPA, and offsets do not replace monthly payments. Pub 131 says applied monies shorten the term. A tax warrant may be filed whether or not an IPA exists. Payments are by automatic bank withdrawal. NOT FOUND: approval time.
sourceDate: DTF IPA info page updated 2025-12-11; Publication 131 (7/25)
establishes: NY IPA mechanics: one-payment grace, 30-day termination notice, interest and penalty continue, refunds offset, new debt needs a new IPA
uncertainty: high confidence on everything stated. 'No setup fee' is inferred from silence (medium confidence). Approval time not found
designImplication: The NY plan is the most forgiving of a single missed payment: treat one miss as recoverable and two in a row as default, followed by a 30-day notice.

claim: DTF bills unpaid tax plus interest and penalty. A Notice and Demand for Payment of Tax Due (DTF-966-E) lets DTF begin collection. Before filing a tax warrant DTF 'will send you notice of the debt and give you an opportunity to resolve it'. A warrant works like a civil judgment and a lien on real and personal property, is filed with the Department of State and the county clerk, and is public. Before a levy, DTF usually sends Form DTF-978, Notice to Judgment Debtor or Obligor. The income execution asks the taxpayer to pay up to 10% of gross wages voluntarily, then has the employer withhold it. Bank accounts and third-party debts can be levied. A driver's license can be suspended for a past-due, fixed and final liability of $10,000 or more, after a 60-day notice and then a DMV 15-day final letter. NOT FOUND: day counts between the bill, the Notice and Demand and the warrant.
sourceDate: Publication 131 (7/25); tax warrants page updated 2025-07-08; IT-201-I (2025)
establishes: NY enforcement tools and thresholds; the notice-to-warrant timing is unpublished
uncertainty: high confidence on the tools and thresholds. DTF-966-E comes from a search snippet of a DTF page. Notice timing not found
designImplication: NY wage garnishment is a fixed 10% of gross, which is easy to model. License suspension starts at $10k, so a small balance never reaches it.

claim: DTF keeps all or part of an overpayment to pay a NYS tax liability, NYC or Yonkers personal income tax, MCTMT, a NYC tax-warrant judgment debt, defaulted state education loans, past-due support, and past-due debts to the IRS and others. Form IT-280 lets a non-obligated spouse protect their share, but not against federal or other-state debts.
sourceDate: 2025 Form IT-201-I, 'Collection of debts from your overpayment (offsets)'
establishes: NY refunds offset NY and NYC balances from any year
uncertainty: high confidence: form instructions
designImplication: Apply a NY refund to the open NY or NYC balance before paying it out.

claim: Pub 131: 'If you have a past due legally enforceable New York State, New York City, or Yonkers income tax debt, it will be referred to the federal government or any state participating in the Multi-State Offset Program. Your federal income tax refund or other state refund may be applied to your New York State tax debt, up to the amount you owe.' The other agency sends prior written notice.
sourceDate: Publication 131 (7/25)
establishes: NY and NYC income tax debts are offset against federal refunds through TOP
uncertainty: high confidence. The NY-specific notice period was not found, but IRC 6402(e) sets a federal minimum of 60 days
designImplication: A NY debt takes the next federal refund.

claim: NOT FOUND: no DTF publication or statute found in this pass says in what order a partial personal income tax payment is applied among tax, penalty and interest.
sourceDate: searched 2026-10-10
establishes: Gap
uncertainty: not found

claim: Any city personal income tax imposed under Article 30 'shall be administered and collected by the commissioner in the same manner as the tax imposed by article twenty-two' (Tax Law 1312(a)). The NYC resident tax is reported, paid, penalized, charged interest, put on IPAs and collected on the IT-201 together with the state tax. IT-201-I lists NYC personal income tax and NYC tax-warrant judgment debts among the debts refunds are offset to. Pub 131 says NYC income tax debts are referred for federal offset.
sourceDate: NY Tax Law 1312(a), nysenate.gov read 2026-10-10; IT-201-I (2025); Pub 131 (7/25)
establishes: NYC resident tax shares the NYS penalty, interest, plan and collection rules
uncertainty: high confidence: statute
designImplication: Add NYC tax to the NY balance and run one penalty, interest and plan engine on the sum. NYC needs no separate collector.

claim: NOT FOUND (and not expected): no separate NYC penalty rate, interest rate or payment plan exists for the resident personal income tax. NYC Department of Finance does not administer it. NYC311 and nyc.gov say DTF administers and collects it.
sourceDate: search result read 2026-10-10 (secondary summary of NYC311)
establishes: There are no NYC-specific collection parameters
uncertainty: medium-high confidence: the statute (1312) is primary; the NYC311 statement came from a search summary
designImplication: Do not model a second collector for NYC.

claim: There is a one-time 5% of the unpaid tax (the underpayment portion), plus 0.5% of the unpaid tax for each month or part of a month it stays unpaid, for at most 40 months. Total cap is 25%. Statute: R&TC 19132.
sourceDate: FTB 'Common penalties and fees' last updated 2026-06-17; FTB 1140 (rev 12/2017)
establishes: CA late-payment penalty = 5% upfront, then 0.5% a month for up to 40 months
uncertainty: high confidence
designImplication: CA combines a one-time charge with a monthly accrual. Model both parts.

claim: If the tax is not paid by the due date and the return is not filed by the extended due date: 5% of the amount due (after timely payments and credits) for each month or part of a month, from the original due date, up to 25%. Individuals have a minimum: if the return shows a balance due, the penalty is the lesser of $135 or 100% of the amount due. A demand penalty of 25% of the total tax (before credits) can be added on top if the taxpayer ignores a Demand for Tax Return. R&TC 19131 and 19133.

value.minimum: lesser of $135 or 100% of amount due

sourceDate: FTB page last updated 2026-06-17
establishes: CA late-filing penalty and its $135 floor
uncertainty: high confidence
designImplication: A small CA balance filed late costs at least $135 or the whole balance. That is a sharp penalty on small debts.

claim: FTB's audit manual: 'If the sum of the penalties assessed under R&TC Sections 19131 and 19133 are greater than the Underpayment Penalty (R&TC Section 19132), then the Underpayment Penalty should not be assessed. See R&TC Section 19132(b).' In effect the taxpayer gets the larger of (delinquent filing + demand) or late payment, not both.
sourceDate: FTB Manual of Audit Procedures ch. 11, Rev. 7/17
establishes: CA late-filing and late-payment penalties do not stack: the larger applies
uncertainty: medium-high confidence: an official FTB manual from 2017. The statute itself was not readable (leginfo blocked the fetch)
designImplication: For a CA late filer, compute both penalties and charge the larger.

claim: Personal income tax underpayment and overpayment interest for 07/01/2026 to 12/31/2026 is 7% a year. Previous rates were 7% (7/1/2025 to 6/30/2026) and 8% (1/1/2025 to 6/30/2025). FTB resets the rate twice a year.
sourceDate: FTB interest rates page, current period 07/01/2026 to 12/31/2026 (read 2026-10-10)
establishes: CA late-2026 rate is 7%
uncertainty: high confidence
designImplication: Use 7% for CA in the second half of 2026, with a semiannual reset.

topic: interest compounding and interest on penalties
claim: Interest is compounded daily (R&TC 19521). It runs on unpaid tax from the original due date and on penalties from the penalty's effective date (R&TC 19101). The audit manual lists daily compounding on 'Unpaid tax ... Interest ... All penalties, except the monthly portion of the late payment of tax penalty'. Interest on the delinquent-filing penalty runs from the return due date; other penalties from the notice date. A full payment within 15 days of the original notice stops further interest after the notice date.
value: daily; on tax, interest and penalties (except monthly late-payment portion)
establishes: CA charges interest on penalties and on interest, compounded daily
uncertainty: high confidence on daily compounding and interest on penalties (several FTB documents agree). The exception for the monthly portion comes from the 2017 manual
designImplication: CA is the only one of the three that compounds on penalties as well, so unpaid CA balances snowball fastest relative to the rate.

claim: The ISR penalty is reported on Form 540 line 92 (FTB 3853). For 2025 it is the larger of a flat amount ($950 per adult, $475 per child under 18, capped at $2,850 per household) or 2.5% of household income above the filing threshold. It is capped at the state average bronze premium ($377 per person per month for 2025). The ISR regulation says FTB's 'civil authority and procedures for collection of income taxes ... shall be applicable to the collection of the penalty', and that the penalty is 'assessed and collected pursuant to Part 10.2'.
sourceDate: FTB 3853 Instructions 2025 (REV 03-26); FTB ISR final regulations (Cal. Code Regs. tit. 18, 26000.61000 et seq.)
establishes: An unpaid ISR penalty goes into the Form 540 balance and is collected like income tax
uncertainty: high confidence on the amounts and on collection under Part 10.2. NOT VERIFIED: whether late-payment penalty and interest apply to an unpaid ISR penalty the same way as to tax. R&TC 61020 was not readable
designImplication: Fold the ISR penalty into the CA balance due. Whether it earns the 19132 penalty is uncertain, so mark the choice as a design assumption.

topic: installment plan eligibility, term, fee, application
claim: Individuals may qualify if the amount due is $25,000 or less, it can be paid in 60 months or less, and all income tax returns for the past 5 years are filed. FTB says 'Typically, you may have up to 3 to 5 years'. Setup fee is $34, added to the balance. Apply online (MyFTB; EFT recurring payments required), by phone 800-689-4776, or by mail on FTB 3567. Online is not available to anyone with a current IA, wage garnishment, bank levy or other collection order; they must call. A financial statement and a state tax lien may be conditions. Larger or longer plans are decided case by case after a financial statement. R&TC 19008(b) requires FTB to accept qualifying requests.
sourceDate: FTB payment plans page last updated 2026-04-07; terms and conditions page last updated 2025-09-24; Collection Procedure Manual 2018
establishes: CA plan: up to $25k, up to 60 months, $34 fee, 5 years of returns filed
uncertainty: high confidence
designImplication: CA offers the longest self-serve plan (60 months) for a small fee. Add the $34 to the balance, where it earns interest.

claim: 'If you apply for a payment plan (installment agreement), it may take up to 90 days to process your request.' Applicants should check status after 2 days if they applied online, or after 90 days on paper. FTB says to keep paying while the request is processed, to limit interest and penalties and to keep the balance from going to collections or wage garnishment. Under R&TC 19008(d)(1), FTB may not levy while an IA request is under review, nor for 30 days after a rejection or during an administrative review of it.
sourceDate: FTB help page last updated 2025-12-17; payment plans page 2026-04-07; FTB 1140
establishes: CA approval takes up to 90 days (about 2 days online), and a request blocks levy while pending
uncertainty: high confidence
designImplication: A pending CA request is a shield: no levy while FTB reviews it. Online approval is near-instant.

topic: installment plan default, accruals, new balances, skip
claim: Penalties and interest keep accruing during the plan, and FTB says a skipped payment's balance 'will continue to accrue interest and penalties'. Terms require filing and paying all future liabilities on time. A dishonored payment can cancel the plan and add a dishonored-payment penalty. Per FTB's Collection Procedure Manual, default includes new liabilities, dishonored payments, missed payments, or death. FTB must mail an Intent to Terminate Installment Agreement notice; the IA ends 30 days later unless the taxpayer requests an administrative review, and collection resumes 30 days after termination. A new balance is a default trigger, not an add-on; the online route excludes anyone with a current IA, so changes go through MyFTB or a call. One payment may be skipped if asked 5 to 30 days before the due date; the term is then extended.
sourceDate: FTB Collection Procedure Manual (Voluntary Case Resolution), last revision 10/2018 (some thresholds redacted); terms page 2025-09-24; help page 2025-12-17
establishes: CA default: Intent to Terminate notice, then 30 days, then termination, then 30 more days before collection. A new debt breaks the plan
uncertainty: medium-high confidence: the manual is official but dated 2018 and redacts how many missed payments trigger default. The skip-a-payment rule is current (2025)
designImplication: CA has a formal cure window of 30 + 30 days before levy. The skip option gives the player one sanctioned miss.

claim: Personal income tax notices, per FTB's Collection Procedure Manual and search excerpts of FTB documents: (1) a Statement of Tax Due or Notice of State Income Tax Due (payable within 15 days with no added interest); (2) the account sits 30 to 45 days in ARCS, then an Income Tax Due Notice (FTB 4963) goes out, warning that unless paid in full within 30 days FTB may impose a collection fee, contact third parties, file liens and take other action; (3) a Final Notice Before Levy and Lien (FTB 4966). The taxpayer may request an administrative review within 30 days of that notice. FTB's description: 'a sequence of three collection letters ... at 30-45 day intervals'. After the final notice, FTB starts wage garnishment (EWOT), bank levies (Order to Withhold, FTB 2900), continuous orders (FTB 2910, effective 12 months) and state tax liens.
sourceDate: FTB Collection Procedure Manual, rev. 10/2018 (exact day counts redacted); FTB 1138 (rev 07-2026); withholding orders page 2025-09-24
establishes: CA: three notices about 30 to 45 days apart, then levy. Roughly 90 to 135 days from the first bill to enforcement
uncertainty: medium confidence: the official manual is from 2018 with redactions. The form numbers 4963 and 4966 come from a search summary of FTB documents. The '30-45 day intervals' sentence is stated for business entities, and individual timing was redacted
designImplication: Schedule CA notices about 30 to 45 days apart, with enforcement no earlier than about 90 days after the first bill.

claim: Enforcement: an Earnings Withholding Order for Taxes (wage garnishment); Orders to Withhold on bank accounts, which collect '100% of all assets available or the entire balance due, whichever is less'; Continuous Orders to Withhold (12 months); interception of state, federal and other-state payments; a statutory lien plus a recorded or filed Notice of State Tax Lien (at least 10 years). Fees for individuals: collection cost recovery fee $362 (07/01/26 onward) when FTB takes involuntary action; filing enforcement fee $143; federal treasury offset fee $23.64; lien fees by county.
sourceDate: FTB penalties and fees page last updated 2026-06-17; withholding orders page 2025-09-24; liens page 2025-09-24
establishes: CA enforcement adds a flat $362 fee and can take a whole bank balance
uncertainty: high confidence
designImplication: The first involuntary CA action adds $362, a lump that hits small debts hardest. A bank levy can sweep the full account.

claim: FTB applies part or all of a refund to a prior balance due (return information notice code 'We applied part or all of the refund ... to a prior balance due'). FTB 1140: unpaid liabilities can be satisfied by intercepting funds due from the federal government, other states or other California agencies (Gov. Code 926.8, 12419-12419.12). The Collection Procedure Manual lists 'Refund applied to any outstanding liabilities'.
sourceDate: FTB 1140 (rev 12/2017); FTB 5949 notice codes (read 2026-10-10, business version); CPM 2018
establishes: A CA refund pays CA balances from other years
uncertainty: high confidence on the practice. The notice-code text quoted is from the business-entity version of FTB 5949; the individual equivalent was not re-read
designImplication: Apply the CA refund to an open CA balance automatically.

claim: FTB partners with Treasury's Bureau of the Fiscal Service. For a past-due, legally enforceable CA income tax debt, FTB sends an Intent to Offset Federal Payments (FTB 1102). If the debt is not paid in full within 60 days, FTB notifies BFS and the federal refund is offset. FTB may charge a federal offset fee ($23.64) and a collection cost recovery fee.
sourceDate: FTB Treasury Offset Program page last updated 2025-09-24
establishes: CA uses TOP after a 60-day notice and charges a fee, unlike CT
uncertainty: high confidence
designImplication: A CA offset of the federal refund costs an extra $23.64.

claim: IRC 6159(a) authorizes the Secretary to agree with a taxpayer to pay 'any tax in installment payments'. The tax meant is tax under the Internal Revenue Code (Title 26). The IRS payment plans page covers only federal 'taxes you owe' plus accrued penalties and interest, and says nothing of state taxes. No IRS text was found that explicitly says 'an IRS plan does not cover state taxes'. The conclusion rests on the statute's scope and the separate state programs.
sourceDate: IRS page last reviewed 2026-08-13; 26 U.S.C. 6159(a) (Cornell LII)
establishes: An IRS installment agreement covers only federal (Title 26) liabilities

designImplication: Keep federal and state plans separate. A federal plan never pays down a state balance.

topic: refund offset to state income tax (6402(e)) and priority
claim: IRC 6402(e)(1) allows offset when a person 'owes a past-due, legally enforceable State income tax obligation' to a state. Under (e)(2) it applies only if the address on the federal return is in the state seeking the offset. Under (e)(4) the state must notify the taxpayer and give at least 60 days to show the debt is not owed. Priority: internal revenue tax (a), then past-due child support (c), then federal agency debts (d), then state income tax (e), then unemployment compensation debts (f). IRS Topic 203 lists 'State income tax obligations' among debts collected through BFS's Treasury Offset Program.
sourceDate: IRS Topic 203 last reviewed 2026-06-01; 26 U.S.C. 6402(e) (Cornell LII)
establishes: A federal refund reaches a state income tax debt only after federal tax, child support and federal agency debts, and only for the state of residence on the return
uncertainty: high confidence on the priority order and the 60-day notice. The residence-address condition (e)(2) was read through a summarizing fetch
designImplication: Waterfall the federal refund: IRS balance, then other priorities, then the home state's tax debt. A CT resident's refund cannot be offset to a CA debt through TOP (6402(e)(2)), only through state-to-state programs.

claim: Beyond TOP, FTB runs a Multistate Offset Program ('Collections for other states'). CT 12-35f lets DRS withhold CT refunds for another state's certified tax debt when that state reciprocates, after a 30-day protest notice. Pub 131 says NY refers debts to 'any state participating in the Multi-State Offset Program'.
sourceDate: FTB collections page last updated 2025-09-27; Conn. Gen. Stat. 12-35f; NY Pub 131 (7/25)
establishes: All three states can reach another state's refund for their tax debts by reciprocity
uncertainty: medium confidence: the mechanism is confirmed for each state. Whether CT, NY and CA have reciprocal agreements with each other was not verified
designImplication: A player who moves states can still lose refunds to an old state's debt. Treat it as optional realism.
